video_title: The Marine Corps' Plan for the Future of Ground Combat
gist: Two Marine officers who co-wrote 'Ground Combat Element 2040' (a 15-year, budget-justifying successor document to Force Design 2030) describe how the Marine Corps is prioritizing layered counter-drone/cruise-missile defense, human-machine teaming, and resilient expeditionary logistics, while explicitly rejecting Russia-Ukraine-style attritional trench warfare and insisting close combat and dismounted infantry remain irreplaceable even as autonomy scales up.

insights.claim: GCE 2040 is a 15-year framework spanning three fiscal year defense programs (FYDPs) out to 2040, built to nest under Force Design 2030 and formally document prioritized, validated ground combat element requirements so the Marine Division can compete for internal Marine Corps resources.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Establishes a multi-year, budget-linked capability roadmap for Marine ground forces, giving contractors a documented long-horizon demand signal tied directly to a resourcing justification.
insights.quote: So three fiscal year defense programs out out to 2040. That's where that moniker comes from.

insights.claim: Inside the Marine Requirements Oversight Council (MROC) budget process, Force Design priorities such as the Marine Littoral Regiment have been getting funded, while other ground-combat-element needs -- especially command-and-control-at-echelon and information-related capability tied to the aviation combat element -- have struggled to secure resources.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Identifies where internal Marine Corps budget competition is creating winners (littoral/sea-denial programs) and laggards (C2/information systems) -- relevant to contractors positioning in either lane.
insights.quote: we were having a really hard time justifying why we needed things.

insights.claim: The document is deliberately written in acquisition-program language (concept, required capabilities) specifically so Marine Corps leaders can use it to justify and resource individual capability requirements in budget fights.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Confirms the document functions as an internal budget-justification instrument rather than pure doctrine, making it a leading indicator of which capabilities get funded next.
insights.quote: concept required capabilities, those words are kind of the acquisition side, the acquisition speak for how you justify a requirement so you can resource it.

insights.claim: Requirements and capability gaps in GCE 2040 are sourced bottom-up through a recurring 'ground board' process in which fleet-level Marines raise problems that get briefed up the chain to the Deputy Commandant for Plans, Policies, and Operations (PP&O) and fed into the Marine Corps Warfighting Lab.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Identifies the actual internal channel through which new capability requirements -- and future contract opportunities -- get validated inside the Marine Corps.

themes.theme: Marine Littoral Regiment: Readiness Gap and Global Reach

insights.claim: Marine Littoral Regiments have not yet been deployed to the current real-world fight and remain in the fielding process, though other force-design-derived capabilities are already contributing to ongoing operations.
insights.speaker: Marine Corps officer (GCE 2040 co-author)
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic fielding timeline for MLR-specific programs (radars, long-range fires, C2/ISR) -- full unit-level capability is still pending, not yet combat-proven.
insights.quote: while the marine latoral regiments have not been deployed to the current fight, there are capabilities that have been developed in support of force design that are contributing to the current fight.

insights.claim: The Marine Littoral Regiment concept -- equipped with radars, long-range fires, anti-air capability, and heavy C2/ISR to deter an adversary fleet in the littorals -- is framed as globally applicable across many maritime choke points, not limited to a single theater.
insights.speaker: Marine Corps officer (GCE 2040 co-author)
insights.so_what: Broadens the addressable mission set (and funding case) for MLR sensor, fires, and C2 systems beyond an Indo-Pacific/China-only scenario.
insights.quote: the Marine Littoral Regiment has applicability with its capabilities worldwide, globally. There there are a lot of lurals.

insights.claim: A Special Purpose MAGTF is currently operating in the SOUTHCOM area of operations landbased and using Navy 'platforms of opportunity' (including at least one LPD) instead of a standard amphibious ready group, explicitly because the Navy does not have enough ships to support the mission.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Direct, current evidence that amphibious ship shortfalls are already forcing improvised force employment -- a structural demand signal for amphibious shipbuilding and sealift capacity.
insights.quote: because we don't have ships enough to put that formation on but they are operating landbased as well as with platforms of opportunity that the Navy can provide.

insights.claim: Adversaries have built large-scale, persistent ISR complexes capable of locating and targeting formations that stay in one place too long, meaning Marine forces 'can no longer set up in a FOB and be safe.'
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Validates continued demand for mobile/dispersed basing, tactical deception, and counter-ISR technology over legacy fixed-base infrastructure.
insights.quote: We know that we can no longer set up in a FOB and be safe.

insights.claim: 'Dominate' is operationally defined as the ability to shoot, move, communicate, and survive with both kinetic and non-kinetic, all-domain (space, cyber, aviation, ground, surface) capability, including a layered, system-of-systems air defense against Group 1-3 drones and cruise missile threats.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Defines a concrete, fundable capability checklist -- layered counter-UAS and counter-cruise-missile defense is an explicit near-term acquisition priority for ground formations.
insights.quote: making sure that we have a layered surface or system of systems air defense so we can defend against the group one through three drone threat as well as deal with some cruise missile threats.

insights.claim: The Corps is deliberately pursuing human-machine teaming so machines assume risk for sensing, shooting, and maneuver instead of Marines, with a stated goal of substantial integration by 2040.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: A long-horizon, budget-backed demand signal for unmanned ground/surface systems and AI/ML-enabled C2 -- stated as a program goal, not speculation.
insights.quote: There is a view that we do not want a human being to be at risk when a machine can assume the risk whether it's for sensing, shooting, maneuver.

insights.claim: Despite the push toward robotics and autonomy, doctrine deliberately stays 'human-centric' (contrasted with the more 'platform-centric' aviation plan) because a 400-scenario historical study of ground combat from WWII to 2022 -- Ben Connable's book 'Ground Combat' -- found close combat to be the one persistent element across all of them.
insights.speaker: Colonel Eric Clark
insights.so_what: A direct counterweight to autonomy/robotics hype -- Marine doctrine assumes irreplaceable dismounted infantry demand (small arms, body armor, close-combat systems) even in a robot- and sensor-heavy future.
insights.quote: the ubiquitousness, the the absolute persistent element in each of those events was was close combat.

insights.claim: Resilience is defined through contested/denied environments: even a high-end asset like the MQ-9 can be shot down by enemy air defense, requiring a layered ISR fallback chain down to a Marine reconnaissance team with only binoculars and a camera able to pass information through the network.
insights.speaker: Colonel Eric Clark
insights.so_what: Argues against reliance on single high-end ISR platforms and for redundant, low-cost/low-signature sensing layers -- relevant to how ISR investment should be diversified across cost tiers.
insights.quote: resilience is the MQ9 that gets taken down by anti- anti-air fire.

themes.theme: Maneuver Warfare Against a Peer Adversary

insights.claim: Marine Corps maneuver warfare doctrine originated in the late 1980s/early 1990s specifically because the Corps expected to be outnumbered and outgunned defending NATO's northern flank against the Soviet army; the same doctrinal logic is now being reapplied against China.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Frames current force design as a doctrinal repeat of a Cold War playbook rather than a new invention -- context for how the Corps expects to fight while outnumbered against China.

insights.claim: The Marine Corps explicitly does not intend to fight like Russia and Ukraine's static, attritional warfare with fixed, slow-moving lines and no air superiority, and instead plans to concentrate maneuver and fires at decisive points and critical vulnerabilities to enable the larger joint force.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: A direct contrast against the most visible current war signals what kind of equipment and doctrine (mobility, precision fires, decisive-point targeting) the Corps is prioritizing over mass/attrition systems.
insights.quote: We we can't go toe-to-toe as a Marine Corps certainly with with an adversary like China.

insights.claim: The document frames a 'decision advantage' cycle -- sense, make sense, communicate, then maneuver/act -- where technology is valued specifically for converting information into operational tempo, not as an end in itself.
insights.speaker: Colonel Eric Clark
insights.so_what: Gives a specific evaluation lens the Marine Corps applies to new C2/sensing/AI products: does it demonstrably increase tempo, not just capability on paper.
insights.quote: Technology not for the sake of technology, technology to turn results into tempo.

insights.claim: In the Russia-Ukraine war, forces can occasionally achieve a tactical breakthrough but cannot exploit it -- a failure attributed to inadequate logistics -- and this is cited as the direct rationale for the Marine Corps prioritizing a resilient, autonomy-enabled logistics network.
insights.speaker: Marine Corps officer (GCE 2040 co-author)
insights.so_what: Positions logistics/resupply automation, not just shooters and sensors, as a core lesson-driven investment priority for the ground combat element.
insights.quote: they might be able to occasionally make a breakthrough, but they can't exploit it.

insights.claim: Bulk fuel and water, and reducing overall power/fuel requirements, are identified as among the hardest operational logistics challenges, driving demand for alternative power sources and smaller, more fuel-efficient vehicles and command-and-control systems.
insights.speaker: Marine Corps officer (GCE 2040 co-author)
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete procurement lane -- compact power generation, fuel-efficient tactical vehicles, and lower-power C2 hardware -- as a stated Marine Corps need.

insights.claim: Individual Marine equipment load has grown to roughly 120 pounds including UAVs, batteries, radios and weapons, with an associated administrative burden of about 15 custody cards and roughly three hours to check gear out of the armory, cited as evidence the Corps must be judged on whether new equipment is actually usable, not just issued.
insights.speaker: Colonel Eric Clark
insights.so_what: A grassroots critique of equipment/procurement bloat -- signals appetite for lighter, better-integrated soldier systems over simply adding more discrete gadgets.
insights.quote: the young Marines out there that are carrying 120 pounds with UAVs and batteries and a radio and a weapon system that now it takes you three hours to check out the armory because you have 15 custody cards.

themes.theme: Doctrinal Humility and a Fast-Moving Threat Picture

insights.claim: The document explicitly states up front that the Marine Corps will 'get the future wrong,' framing adaptability and resilience -- not predictive accuracy -- as the actual goal of the 2040 planning horizon.
insights.speaker: Colonel Eric Clark
insights.so_what: Signals the plan is designed for continuous revision rather than fixed execution -- expect requirements to shift with feedback loops rather than lock in for 15 years.
insights.quote: the document admits up front, we're going to get the future wrong. Everybody gets the future wrong.

insights.claim: Just five years before this conversation, nobody anticipated the scale of proliferation of first-person-view one-way attack drones, how contested the electromagnetic spectrum would become, or the need to defend simultaneously against ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones.
insights.speaker: Major General Jason Morris
insights.so_what: Explicit admission of a doctrine-lag problem -- supports the urgency case for counter-UAS, electronic warfare, and integrated air/missile defense investment as capability gaps the Corps knows it hasn't closed.
insights.quote: 5 years ago, I don't think any of us would have even thought about the proliferation of firstperson view one-way attack drones.
